assessment.security_status_cs: Bezpečnostní situace v regionu prudce eskaluje po úspěšných útocích Houthiů na ropné provozy a vojenskou infrastrukturu v Saúdské Arábii včetně sestřeleného proudového letounu. Multilaterální námořní koalice se sice snaží zabezpečit trasy v Rudém moři a úžině Bab al-Mandab, avšak pokračující útoky na tankery a uzavření klíčového ropovodu drží globální energetické trhy ve stavu vysoké pohotovosti.
assessment.security_status_en: The security situation in the region is escalating sharply following successful Houthi strikes on oil infrastructure and military assets in Saudi Arabia, including a downed fighter jet. While a multinational naval coalition is attempting to secure routes in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait, continued attacks on tankers and the closure of a crucial oil pipeline keep global energy markets on high alert.

recommendations.reason_en: Persistent threats in the Bab al-Mandab strait and ongoing blockages force carriers to route around Africa, keeping freight rates elevated.

articles.title: Battle of Chile director Patricio Guzmán dies aged 85
articles.summary:
Passionate documentary maker won international acclaim for unsparing but poetic films exploring the impact of the Pinochet regime in Chile

Patricio Guzmán, the film-maker who chronicled Chile’s bloody 1970s political strife and its subsequent social and political turmoil in films such as The Battle of Chile and Nostalgia for the Light, has died aged 85. According to Chilean news outlet Emol, Guzmán died on Tuesday in Paris after a cardiorespiratory arrest.

Guzmán’s chief preoccupation throughout his career was the carnage unleashed by Augusto Pinochet’s coup in 1973 against Salvador Allende, Chile’s elected president. He later told the Guardian: “I’m a film-maker who was very marked by the ways of the dictator. It has remained with me for ever. I cannot leave it behind.” However, he resisted the idea that he was an activist, political film-maker, adding: “I’m not a sociologist. Neither am I a politician. I make films that are metaphorical and poetic; I interpret reality through my own personal way of looking.”

articles.title: Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces launch inquest into sudden military collapse
articles.summary:
Rout raises questions about coordination and morale as some politicians claim billions of dollars were offered to persuade forces to abandon position

A bitter inquest is under way among Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces as to how what was being billed as a decisive assault on Sana’a, the Houthi-controlled capital, suddenly collapsed into a military rout.

More than 15 brigades were defeated as the country’s entire west coast fell into Houthi hands. Efforts are now being made to reorganise the anti-Houthi forces representing the UN-recognised Yemeni government in order to capture the Kahbob mountains, a strategic point from which to restrict Houthi forces moving closer to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait.

articles.title: Israel seeks US weapons 'compensation' after Saudi F-35 deal
articles.summary:
Israel seeks US weapons 'compensation' after Saudi F-35 deal

Submitted by MEE staff on Sat, 09/19/2026 - 11:50
Tel Aviv reportedly wants advanced systems to preserve its military edge after Washington approved 48 F-35s for Riyadh
A US Air Force F-35 is displayed during the Paris Air Show at Le Bourget Airport near Paris, 15 June 2025 (Thomas Samson/AFP)
Off

Israel plans to seek additional US weapons and defence capabilities as "compensation" after Washington approved the potential sale of F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, Israeli media has reported.

Israeli news website Walla reported on Friday that Israeli officials are expected to ask US President Donald Trump's administration to approve weapons systems that Washington had previously declined to provide.

The reported requests extend beyond advanced fighter aircraft and stealth capabilities to space-based weapons and the development and production of interceptor aircraft, Walla reported.

Israeli officials are also expected to seek "bunker-busting munitions and underground systems capable of operating deep beneath rocky mountains".

Walla said the requests are intended to secure a US "compensation" package following Washington's decision to approve the potential F-35 sale to Riyadh.

The report comes after the US State Department approved a possible $24.3bn sale of 48 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets to Saudi Arabia.

The proposed package also includes 49 Pratt & Whitney F135-PW-100 engines, communications and cryptographic equipment, electronic warfare support, training and logistics, according to the State Department's notification to Congress.

The proposed sale still requires congressional approval.

Middle East Eye has reported on the progress of the sale for months, with multiple US and Arab sources saying it was moving quickly.

MEE revealed in November that Saudi Arabia's F-35 purchase would be "fast-tracked" under a new defence partnership with the US, sealed during Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's visit to the White House. 

US says it will sell up to 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia
Read More »

MEE then revealed in December that the Trump administration was conducting a review of Israel's "qualitative military edge" as part of the process.  

Senior US military officials held several closely guarded meetings on Capitol Hill to discuss the sale at the start of the year.

Saudi Arabian Defence Minister Khaled bin Salman visited the US multiple times this summer, in part to ensure the deal went through, US officials told MEE. 

If completed, Saudi Arabia would become the first Arab country to operate F-35s, while Israel is currently the only Middle Eastern country operating the aircraft. 

Reuters news agency reported that the proposed sale could test Washington's longstanding policy of maintaining Israel's qualitative military edge in the region.

Saudi Arabia is reeling from Houthi missile and drone attacks while its allies in Yemen, the internationally recognised government, are struggling to stem a Houthi offensive that has resulted in them securing the entirety of Yemen's Red Sea coastline, along with the Arabian Gulf side of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

Pakistan and Iran foreign ministers discuss regional stability and safe shipping

Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, spoke by phone to discuss recent regional developments, Islamabad confirmed in a statement.

The two diplomats agreed to maintain close cooperation and are scheduled to meet in person in New York on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly.

articles.title: Gaza's children with Down syndrome struggle to rebuild skills lost to genocide
articles.summary:
Gaza's children with Down syndrome struggle to rebuild skills lost to genocide 

Submitted by Abdallah al-Naami on Fri, 09/18/2026 - 11:03
Displacement, trauma and destroyed care centres force children and their families to start again amid an ongoing humanitarian crisis
A child with Down syndrome smiles during a class held inside a makeshift tent in central Gaza (MEE/Abdallah al-Naami)
Off

After a long walk through displacement camps and dusty roads, 13-year-old Heba Alataar arrives exhausted at her class at the Right to Live Society (RLS) centre in al-Zawaida, central Gaza.

Inside a small makeshift tent divided into two classrooms, the Palestinin girl sits on the ground alongside her classmates, all children with Down syndrome, as they try to learn new skills.

Alataar is one of more than 1,000 children with Down syndrome in Gaza.

Like all children in Gaza, they have paid a heavy toll during Israel's genocide.

But the conflict has been especially destructive for these children. 

Israeli attacks have destroyed the institutions that provided their education and care, erasing skills they spent years developing.

Children and their families are now struggling to rebuild their skills and lives amid displacement, trauma and a severe lack of resources.

Life before the genocide

Before the war, many children with Down syndrome in Gaza had access to specialised care from birth through adulthood, mainly through the Right to Live Society.

Founded in 1993, RLS operated three facilities across Gaza and employed 200 staff members.

Raoufa Salama, director of rehabilitation programmes, told Middle East Eye that its services included early intervention, education and rehabilitation programmes, as well as psychological counselling for parents.

For Heba's father, Alaa Alattar, that support was life-changing.

“When I found out my daughter had Down syndrome, I cried for days. I didn't know about her condition or how to raise her. I was worried about her future,” Alattar told MEE.

 “All my fears and worries vanished when we visited RLS and saw the care the children receive and the level of skills they achieved.”

By the age of 10, Heba had mastered basic skills including comprehension, speech and personal hygiene. She was also beginning to learn to read and write.

 “I was delighted and proud of my daughter's progress,” Alattar said. “I was starting to picture a bright future for her.”

But her progress was interrupted when Israeli attacks began in October 2023.

Major setbacks

Israeli attacks destroyed all RLS facilities and killed many children with Down syndrome, while others remain missing.

Those who survived the bombing faced constant terror and harsh conditions in displacement.

Nabila Abed Rabbo recalled how each wave of bombardment left her 13-year-old daughter, Saja Abed Rabbo, gripped by fear.

"Every time my daughter heard an explosion, she became terrified. She tried to cover her ears and came to me screaming and insisting on staying by my side,” Abed Rabbo told MEE.

“Because of the constant fear and the catastrophic living conditions in displacement, Saja has lost all her basic skills. She couldn't even use the toilet. We had to rely on diapers, which were extremely difficult to provide because of the blockade.”

 For Alattar, watching his daughter lose her skills was devastating.

'There are no words to describe the heartbreak I felt... to see my little girl depressed and sitting alone in displacement'

- Alaa Alattar, Palestinian father 

“The war took everything from Heba. She lost all her skills, interests and routine. She returned to square one, as if she never received any education or care,” the Palestinian father said, his voice breaking with emotion.

“There are no words to describe the heartbreak I felt as a father to see years of my daughter's hard work and the dedicated efforts of her teachers and family vanish in the blink of an eye, to see my little girl depressed and sitting alone in displacement.”

For other families, the disruption was just as profound. Bahjat Sultan said his 14-year-old daughter, Fatima, suffered as a result of the bombing, displacement and separation from her educational environment.

“The war affected Fatima deeply. She lost the ability to express her feelings and began showing aggressive behaviour," Bahjat told MEE.

"Even at night, she struggled to sleep and often woke up terrified and crying from nightmares.” 

Salama said the trauma of war has taken a heavy psychological toll on children with Down syndrome in Gaza, causing major setbacks in skills such as communication and personal hygiene.

She also said there had been a rapid increase in births of children with Down syndrome in Gaza. The RLS centre in Al-Zawaida now receives four to five new cases a week, compared with one to two before the war.

Salama attributed the increase to exposure to high levels of pollution from Israeli explosives and psychological stress.

Rebuilding amid destruction

Despite their suffering, children have held on to memories of RLS.

Throughout her family's repeated displacement across Gaza, Fatima Sultan made sure to carry her RLS uniform in her bag.

Gaza's children face genetic harm 'for generations to come' from Israel's genocide
Read More »

“Fatima would often wear her uniform and ask me to take her to the centre. I kept promising to take her later, hoping that education would resume one day,” her father said.

In July 2024, the RLS team began efforts to resume some of its services. Salama said the aim was to provide psychological support to parents and children, help them regain lost skills and, most importantly, raise awareness about the dangers associated with war and displacement.

The activities began with recreational events and home visits, and later expanded to include early intervention, educational and rehabilitation programmes.

News of RLS's return brought joy to families and children.

“I tried to enrol Saja in several schools, but she was rejected because of her condition,” said Abed Rabbo.

“When we received the invitation from RLS, she was so happy that she could finally go to her own school, learn and make friends.”

Today, RLS provides services to more than 1,000 children with Down syndrome and autism in makeshift tents at three locations across the Gaza Strip.

Because of the destruction and blockade, Salama said there is a severe shortage of essential resources, including suitable educational environments and equipment.

To cope with the shortage, teachers make educational materials using cardboard from aid packages and coloured paper.

According to Salama, ongoing Israeli attacks remain the biggest challenge to the rehabilitation process. Children risk losing newly regained skills as a result of trauma from air strikes and displacement.

Despite a ceasefire announced in October last year, Israel has continued to carry out near-daily attacks across Gaza and maintained severe restrictions on the entry of aid.

Israeli forces have killed at least 1,386 Palestinians since the ceasefire was announced, including at least 300 children.

Hundreds more have been wounded, including RLS student Ahmed Al-Mabhouh, 14, who was shot five times by an Israeli soldier while playing near his home east of Al-Bureij refugee camp. The shooting left him severely wounded and unable to attend his classes.

Hope through education

Despite the immense challenges, the children are gradually making progress.

Salama said children and their families remain committed to the rehabilitation process. They are regaining vital skills such as communication and personal hygiene, while beginning to learn to read and write and to recognise and avoid danger. 

Since reuniting with RLS, Heba's life has changed, according to her father. Learning has become part of her daily routine.

“Learning became a new lifestyle for Heba. It occupies most of her time. She is always excited to go to the centre and loves to tell us about her friends and what she learned,” he said.

“She became happier and more focused. We are grateful for the devoted efforts of the RLS team.”

For Alattar, seeing his daughter make progress again has renewed his hopes.

“I hope that the war truly ends and our children no longer fear air strikes or sudden displacement,” he said.

“I hope for my daughter to have a safe educational environment that helps her recover, thrive and grow up to achieve our dream of becoming a teacher for children with Down syndrome.”

Israel's genocide in Gaza

articles.title: Morning recap
articles.summary:
Morning recap

Good morning Middle East Eye readers,
If you're just joining us, here are key developments from across the region:

•    US President Donald Trump has signed into law legislation extending existing US sanctions on Iran to 2031 and expanding sanctions, tariffs and other restrictions on Russia.

•    Explosions were heard in Riyadh on Saturday, AFP reported, while Saudi civil defence authorities issued, and later withdrew, alerts for several provinces.

•    Yemen’s Human Rights Ministry accused the Houthis of attacking and looting Saudi-funded humanitarian and medical facilities in al-Khawkhah and other areas along the western coast of the country.

•    Yemen's Houthis said that Saudi Arabia had launched 26 strikes against areas under their control in the past 24 hours, amid continuing fighting between the Iran-aligned movement and Yemen's Riyadh-backed government.

•    Turkey has revoked the operating licence of Iran’s Bank Mellat, which remains on the US Treasury’s sanctions list, as Washington intensifies economic pressure on Tehran.

•    Saudi Arabia has informed at least two oil refining customers in Europe that they will not receive crude oil allocations in October, as the war in the Middle East hits global energy markets. 

•    Former Palestinian Authority minister, Sufian Abu Zaida, has said he acted as a go-between for Israel and Hamas before 7 October 2023, and has promised to disclose the message Yahya Sinwar asked him to pass on.

•    Three Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks in the Gaza Strip, Al Jazeera reported, citing local hospital sources.

•    Yemen’s foreign minister, Afrah Alzouba, has said that Yemen is not “an Iranian bargaining chip” and that its future is “determined by Yemenis through their state and national path”.

•    Rear Admiral Abdullah bin Salem al-Shehri, commander of the Multinational Maritime Defence Coalition (MMDC), has said that protection of international waterways is an international responsibility, and warned that “any threat to international maritime security will be deterred”.

•    US Central Command (Centcom) said it has redirected 105 commercial vessels since the US enforced a naval blockade against Iran.

articles.title: Saudi commander says security of international waterways collective responsibility
articles.summary:
Saudi commander says security of international waterways collective responsibility

Rear Admiral Abdullah bin Salem al-Shehri, commander of the Multinational Maritime Defence Coalition (MMDC), has said that protection of international waterways is an international responsibility, and warned that “any threat to international maritime security will be deterred”.

Al Shehri was addressing the press after the coalition’s fourth planning meeting concluded in Jeddah on Friday.
 
The MMDC is a 14-country military alliance formed in July to ensure global waterways around the Arabian Peninsula, including the Gulf of Aden, the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, and the Red Sea, remain open to international traffic.

The meeting in Jeddah was part of the coalition’s "ongoing transition from the founding stage to the actual operational stage, having reached Initial operational capability," the ministry said in a statement on X.

The meeting was attended by representatives of "41 brotherly and friendly countries," and EU representatives also took part.

articles.title: 'Yemen not Iranian bargaining chip', foreign minister says
articles.summary:
'Yemen not Iranian bargaining chip', foreign minister says

Yemen’s foreign minister, Afrah Alzouba, has said that Yemen is not “an Iranian bargaining chip” and that its future is “determined by Yemenis through their state and national path”.

In a discussion with Russian news agency, Sputnik, Alzouba emphasized that restoring the state is a “pillar for regional security and the protection of international navigation”, according to statement posted on X by the country’s foreign ministry. 

The post said that during the discussion, Alzouba addressed the escalation by “the terrorist Houthi militia” in the western coast and Bab al-Mandab, its humanitarian repercussions, its implications for national and regional security, and international trade routes, as well as relations with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

archive.security_status: Bezpečnostní situace v regionu prudce eskaluje po bleskové vojenské operaci Húthiů podél jemenského pobřeží Rudého moře a úspěšných údronech a raketových útocích na saúdská ropná zařízení. Útoky v Hormuzském průlivu a rostoucí riziko zapojení regionálních sil (Pakistán, Egypt) posouvají konflikt do fáze přímého ohrožení globální energetické infrastruktury.
archive.forecast: V nejbližších dnech lze očekávat pokračující extrémní volatilitu cen ropy, růst nákladů na námořní pojištění a zvýšenou diplomatickou i vojenskou aktivitu koaličních sil v Rudém moři.

archive.security_status: Situace v oblasti Rudého moře a Hormuzského průlivu eskaluje po bleskové vojenské ofenzivě Húthíů, útocích na ropovod v Saúdské Arábii a napadení ropného tankeru v Perském zálivu. Došlo k výpadku klíčové infrastruktury a dodávek ropy v řádu milionů barelů denně, což bezprostředně ohrožuje globální energetickou bezpečnost.
archive.forecast: V nejbližších dnech lze očekávat setrvání cen ropy na vysokých úrovních, zvýšené napětí kolem námořních tras a intenzivní diplomatické manévry USA a Saúdské Arábie. Volatilita na trzích zůstane kvůli fyzickým výpadkům dodávek extrémní.

archive.security_status: Bezpečnostní situace v regionu eskalovala na kritickou úroveň v důsledku bleskové ofenzívy Húthíů, kteří ovládli celé jemenské pobřeží Rudého moře a úžinu Bab el-Mandeb. Klíčový saúdský ropovod byl uzavřen po dronovém útoku a incidenty v Hormuzském průlivu a Rudém moři vážně ohrožují globální námořní trasy a energetickou infrastrukturu.
archive.forecast: V nejbližších dnech lze očekávat extrémní volatilitu cen ropy, pokračující útoky na energetickou infrastrukturu a zesílené vojenské i diplomatické aktivity USA v regionu.

archive.security_status: Situace v regionu eskaluje na několika frontách současně. Húthíové provedli úspěšný bleskový postup a ovládli celé jemenské pobřeží Rudého moře i úžinu Bab al-Mandeb, zatímco útoky dronů a raket vážně poškodily klíčové saúdské ropovodní trasy a tankery v Perském zálivu.
archive.forecast: V nejbližších dnech lze očekávat další eskalaci napětí v Rudém moři a Hormuzském průlivu, přičemž ceny ropy a zemního plynu zůstanou pod silným růstovým tlakem.

archive.security_status: Situace v Rudém moři a okolí dosáhla kritického bodu po úspěšné ofenzívě Húthíů u pobřeží Bab al-Mandeb a útocích na klíčovou saúdskou ropnou infrastrukturu včetně ropovodu a přístavu Yanbu. Konflikt eskaluje do regionální roviny za účasti regionálních mocností a narušuje globální energetické toky.
